cards.title: Core idea
cards.body: A database stores data durably and lets many clients read and write it concurrently and correctly. A single node, such as one PostgreSQL or MySQL server, gives tables, indexes, SQL and ACID transactions.

cards.title: How it works
cards.body: At scale one node is not enough. Replication adds availability and read scaling but brings replication lag and consistency trade-offs. Partitioning or sharding adds write throughput and size but makes cross-partition queries and transactions harder. Each step removes one limit and creates the next problem.

questions.q: When a single database struggles, should you shard right away?
questions.a: No. Sharding is the last lever because it permanently adds cross-shard joins, rebalancing and a hard-to-change partition key. Optimize, scale up and add replicas first.

questions.q: What does replication add, and what does it cost?
questions.a: Availability and read scaling, at the cost of replication lag and consistency trade-offs.

questions.q: What does sharding add, and what does it cost?
questions.a: Write throughput and data size, at the cost of harder cross-partition queries and transactions.
